items.title: A 32K-window proxy that beat full context on long agent histories
items.story_key: story|title:a 32k window proxy that beat full context on long agent histories
items.content_excerpt: Like Johnny, your local agent carries more than its head can hold — and keeps working for hours. Transparent proxy: verbatim archive, structured recall, segments, saved engine state. Like Johnny, your agent carries more than its head can hold — and keeps working for hours. A transparent HTTP proxy that sits between a coding agent and a local model (llama.cpp's llama-server , Strata , ds4-server , or any OpenAI-compatible server). The agent keeps sending its whole, unmodified history; the proxy decides what the model actually reads. Old material leaves the prompt but is never summarized away: every message, tool call and output stays on disk, verbatim, and the model can pull any of it back. It speaks OpenAI Chat Completions, Anthropic Messages and OpenAI Responses. Python ≥ 3.10, standard library only. Developed and benchmarked primarily with Strata , by Niko1221 and contributors. mnemonic-proxy is an independently maintained project that also supports llama-server, ds4-server and other OpenAI-compatible backends; saved engine state depends on what the backend supports (see Engines ). Measured on our hardware (single runs, see What we have not proven ): a 3 h 15 min coding session on one 12 GB GPU with 448K tokens of history and at most 105K in the prompt ( One session, measured ); AgentLongBench in a 32K window, 86/100 right with the proxy vs 47 with an LLM summary and 69 with the full history in a larger window ( benchmark ); a 110K-token conversation resumed from disk in 1.4 s instead of ≈50 s ( Saved state, measured ). check ends with READY (exit 0) or says, line by line, what to change; --live adds a real generation, a tool call and a save/restore. --upstream is the engine's address. Then point the agent at the proxy (port 8096) instead of the engine. The engine window must be at least 16K tokens, 32K or more recommended ( Requirements ). items.story_key: story|ver:10.0|title:devin agent skills that patch the gitlab cvss 10 0 php and node js rces
items.content_excerpt: Three Agent Skills that find and patch vulnerable runtimes across your repos. They work in any coding agent that reads SKILL.md files: Devin, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Factory Droid, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Windsurf and 70 more . The CLI detects the agents on your machine and asks where to install. Add -g to install for every project, or pick agents directly: The repo carries a Codex plugin manifest ( .codex-plugin/plugin.json ) and marketplace ( .agents/plugins/marketplace.json ). Add it as a marketplace in Codex, then install Vulnerability Fixes from /plugins . Codex also reads .agents/skills/ , so npx skills add CognitionAI/devin-vuln-fixes -a codex works without the plugin. Droid also reads skills that npx skills add -a droid installs into .agents/skills/ . Copy a skill folder into your agent's skills directory. The common locations are .agents/skills/ , .claude/skills/ , .devin/skills/ , .factory/skills/ and .windsurf/skills/ : Or invoke directly where your agent supports slash commands: /fix-php-vuln , /fix-node-vuln , /fix-gitlab-vuln . The agent needs read access to the repos, and for the build and test steps it needs Docker and access to the image registry or package mirror your CI already uses. When public hosts are blocked, the skills tell the agent to mark a target as unverified and let CI prove it. The fixed-version numbers are pinned to the advisories of October 21, 2026. When a vendor ships a newer patch, we update the skill and bump metadata.version in its frontmatter. See CHANGELOG.md . Run npx skills update to pick up changes; skills-lock.json records the hash you have.

items.story_key: story|title:the fastest most token efficient ios simulator mcp for ai agents
items.content_excerpt: Simulator use for agents: read and drive the iOS Simulator from any MCP client or the command line. The fastest, most token-efficient way for an AI agent to use the iOS Simulator. simulator-use gives Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and any other MCP client a phone: it builds and runs your Xcode project, reads the screen as a few lines of text, taps and types by label, and runs your tests case by case. Its own native engine talks to the Simulator directly, so reading the whole screen takes about 250 ms and a tap goes out in under a millisecond, where tools that start a helper for every call take 1.5 to 3 seconds. Free and open source (MIT), on any Mac with Xcode, and from Linux, Windows or a Mac without Xcode through a cloud iPhone. It builds, runs and tests Xcode projects, reads and uses the screen of any app (SwiftUI, UIKit, React Native), answers iOS's permission prompts, reads the app's logs and crashes, and records video. ui_act takes steps in the same words ui_look prints, runs them in order, and answers with what changed: The MCP server and the CLI are built from one list, so they always match. The tool list and instructions stay under 4,000 tokens; a test enforces it. app_run does the whole loop in one call: it finds the project (a workspace first, then a project, an XcodeGen spec, or ios/ ), picks the scheme, builds for the Simulator, installs, launches, and answers with the first screen. The app's permissions are granted when it is installed and its first launch's prompts (notifications too) are answered, so no prompt stops the agent; permissions: "ask" keeps iOS's prompts, to test them. open_url answers iOS's "Open in …?" for a link that opens another app. tests_run runs the scheme's tests and reads the answer from Xcode's result bundle, not from the scrolling output: app_logs shows what the app itself said, not the thousands of lines Apple's frameworks log from inside it: Agents that run simulator-use through a shell, a command per call, get the same tools: No Mac? If your agent works on Linux, Windows or in a cloud sandbox, NoMac gives it a real Mac in the cloud, with Xcode and the iOS Simulator, billed by the minute. Any other client: run npx -y simulator-use mcp as a stdio server. It speaks MCP 2024-11-05 through 2026-07-28. Agents that work from a shell can use the CLI instead; skill/SKILL.md in the package teaches it in under 2 KB. items.title: When LLMs Forget What They Believe: Characterizing State Integrity Collapse in Long-Horizon Dialogues
items.summary: Large language models can repeat an instruction while failing to keep obeying it. We study this recall-compliance dissociation in long-horizon dialogue and define State Integrity Collapse: a model preserves a stated constraint in memory but stops applying it to later turns. We introduce StateTrack-Bench, a controlled suite of conversations covering numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical-rule constraints. Across seven provider-pinned model snapshots and five dialogue-depth probes, strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, with degradation concentrated in symbolic constraints and in one especially brittle model. A forked recall audit shows that 88.6% of observed failures are behavioral-drift failures rather than ordinary forgetting; excluding the brittle outlier preserves this diagnosis (84.4% of failures). Extended evaluations at depths up to 50 turns confirm that the dissociation persists beyond the core benchmark, while Structured State Anchoring recovers up to 24.4 points on immutable constraints. The results show that reliability cannot be inferred from single-turn instruction following alone; evaluation must track whether remembered constraints remain operational as dialogue state grows. Code and artifacts are available at: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/StateTrack.

items.title: Adaptive Skill Granularity for Coding Agents: Runtime Routing and Macro-to-Micro Recovery
items.summary: Reusable skills allow large language model agents to package task-specific procedures, tool affordances, and execution guidance into modular units. Prior work has largely studied how agents retrieve, compose, or synthesize skills before execution. In coding agents, however, execution poses an additional runtime control problem: the same task may be solved through primitive tool calls, macro skills, or hybrid execution that starts with a macro and falls back to micro-level recovery. We introduce Adaptive Skill Granularity, a framework that treats skill granularity as an action-abstraction policy conditioned on task structure, execution state, and macro-skill failures. The system combines a feature-based granularity controller and a finite-state recovery executor. We evaluate the framework with a deterministic coding-agent protocol using verifier-defined success, total cost, and process metrics such as macro adoption, failure recovery, route match, and transition correctness. Results show that fixed macro execution is efficient when applicable but brittle under mismatch, while runtime routing and explicit macro-to-micro recovery improve robustness and recover controlled macro failures that fixed-granularity execution leaves unresolved. Our findings suggest that skill libraries for coding agents should be treated not only as retrievable resources, but also as controllable, verifiable, and recoverable execution abstractions.

items.title: SABLE: Scalable Affine Bayesian Latent-space Exploration
items.summary: Complex objects such as engineering designs and proteins are often difficult to optimise because their design spaces exhibit high-dimensional structure and objective evaluations are expensive. Generative models provide continuous latent representations, but their latent spaces can have thousands to tens of thousands of dimensions, creating a regime where the latent dimension $D$ greatly exceeds the evaluation budget. We introduce SABLE, a Bayesian optimisation method for high-dimensional latent spaces with an isotropic distribution and limited budget. SABLE uses a Bayesian affine surrogate for prediction and acquisition, treating higher-order structure as surrogate discrepancy. After $N$ observations, the slope update has dimension at most $N-1$, yielding a decomposition of each query into an in-span component optimised by expected improvement (EI) in at most $N$ dimensions and an off-span component governed by a scalar norm. We show that the off-span norm implicitly selected by affine EI can lead to underexploration, and SABLE instead prescribes it using a finite-horizon schedule, without restricting search to a learned subspace. A recompression scheme reduces information to $\mathcal O(M)$ pseudo-observations, bounding refitting cost by $\mathcal O(M^2D+M^3)$ while keeping parameter inference, prediction, and acquisition decisions to tens of milliseconds. Across synthetic benchmarks and latent-space optimisation tasks, SABLE achieves high sample efficiency and reduces decision time by several orders of magnitude at large budgets.

items.title: Scaling Kimi K3 on AMD Instinct MI355X: Matching NVIDIA HGX B300 Throughput per GPU on AgentX
items.summary: Inside the Kimi K3 optimization effort: understanding the bottlenecks and the decisions that made inference faster
items.story_key: model:kimi|title:scaling kimi k3 on amd instinct mi355x matching nvidia hgx b300 throughput per g
items.content_excerpt: Inside the Kimi K3 optimization effort: understanding the bottlenecks and the decisions that made inference faster On AgentX, an eight-GPU AMD Instinct MI355X system serving Kimi K3 with vLLM delivers 24.4% more total tokens per second per GPU than NVIDIA HGX B300 at 50 tokens/s/user P90 interactivity. Under the benchmark’s ownership-cost model, it delivers 87.4% more tokens per dollar . In this post, we’ll unpack the engineering behind Kimi K3 on AMD Instinct MI355X, connecting vLLM’s serving decisions to GPU kernels and the hardware underneath. We’ll explain why the optimizations worked and build the intuition to spot wasted work, identify bottlenecks and find the next optimization in your own inference stack. Interactivity is reciprocal P90 response inter-token latency and excludes time to first token. Total tokens include reused input and generated output. Source: SemiAnalysis InferenceX , October 9, 2026 snapshot. Comparison configurations . Published dense matrix peaks are 10.1 PFLOP/s MXFP4 for AMD Instinct MI355X and 13.5 PFLOP/s FP4 for NVIDIA B300. Both have 288 GB HBM3E and 8 TB/s peak memory bandwidth. Reaching this serving performance reflects sustained software engineering by AMD and collaborators across the vLLM community. The public AgentX benchmark replays real coding-agent session traces with synthetic tokens, retaining request lengths, timing and prefix-sharing patterns. The workload offers over 96% theoretical prefix reuse with unlimited cache. Speculative runs use a fixed synthetic acceptance reference. At 50 tokens/s/user P90 interactivity , AMD Instinct MI355X serves approximately 7,567 total tokens/s/GPU , compared with 6,083 for NVIDIA HGX B300 , a 24.4% throughput advantage . Using SemiAnalysis’s modeled TCO of $1.50 versus $2.26 per GPU-hour , respectively, that translates to 18.16 million versus 9.69 million total tokens per dollar of TCO: 87.4% more tokens per dollar . SemiAnalysis InferenceX public curves, with the 50 tokens/s/user target annotated. Benchmark notes . The public curves compare complete serving stacks. The measurements beside each optimization come from separate tests and explain individual mechanisms under their stated configurations. items.title: claude-code v2.1.307
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added /claude-api api-version to move Claude API code to API version 2026-10-21
  • Added the claude_code.safety_event OpenTelemetry event for each tool call a permission rule, auto mode, a safety check, a hook or the sandbox stopped, prompted or sent back
  • Fixed requests failing with a model-not-found error when CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT is set and the model is an alias with the [1m] suffix, such as opus[1m]
  • Fixed the prompt-caching-scope beta header being sent behind custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL gateways and on Foundry, where it has no effect
  • Fixed MCP servers showing "needs authentication" in claude -p on macOS while the login keychain was locked; they now say why, and the next run after an unlock connects without a new sign-in
  • Fixed MCP servers being reported as timed out, and staying failed in headless runs, when a macOS or Linux computer went to sleep while they were connecting
  • Fixed HTTP MCP tool calls being sent twice when the connection closed mid-call; only read-only or idempotent tools are now retried
  • Fixed a turn sometimes starting without an SDK MCP server's latest tools when a background task was running
  • Fixed some "Autocompact is thrashing" errors in turns that read many PDF pages, images or other large tool results
  • Fixed /autocompact in cloud sessions going back to the default window after the session restarted
  • Fixed a conversation cleared with /clear sometimes coming back when a cloud or self-hosted runner session restarted
  • Fixed CLAUDE_STREAM_FIRST_BYTE_TIMEOUT_MS being ignored in Claude apps gateway sessions
  • Fixed telemetry from Claude Desktop sessions behind a Claude apps gateway being rejected when OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS is set
  • Fixed /permissions > Recently denied not showing the denied shell command, and auto mode's local classifier ignoring an approval from there when it checks a retried command; approving a row now names the command, not its description
  • Fixed /help and the / command menu showing long model-facing descriptions for bundled skills such as /claude-api instead of their short descriptions
  • Fixed subagent transcripts recording placeholder token usage and an empty stop reason for streamed responses
  • Fixed model switches through the Agent SDK's setModel(), and apps built on it, being refused when the API took more than 5 seconds to confirm the model; Claude Code now waits up to 15 seconds
  • Fixed a background command stopped through a connected app (such as the desktop app archiving an idle session) being reported to Claude as stopped by the user; the notice now names its output file
  • Fixed WebFetch in Cowork cloud sessions reporting a tool error when a site answered with a 4xx status or a robots.txt refusal; it is now a normal result, as in local sessions
  • Fixed write tools on a directly configured GitHub MCP server showing a form that closed without creating anything in the desktop app's Code tab
  • Fixed Artifact tool reads failing with a connection reset when the server had closed a reused connection
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions with --use-anthropic-git-proxy committing a .claude/settings.local.json left in the clone by an earlier session
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed archiving or requeueing a session, or stopping the runner, during its checkout hook leaving the hook's processes running and the runner's slot held
  • Improved recovery from unparseable tool calls: Claude Code now retries the call up to twice before ending the turn with an error
  • Improved fork subagents launched together: each is now told which launch is its own, so forks are much less likely to try to start each other's work
  • Improved browser sign-in: the success page now appears as soon as sign-in completes, without waiting for your account profile to load
  • Improved web search errors in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions: a search refused with a 403 that gives a reason now shows that reason instead of a generic "Authentication error"
  • Improved the time to the first reply in cloud sessions when one of the desktop app's MCP servers can't connect
  • Improved Remote Control connect time for sessions whose transcript contains large pasted images or PDF reads
  • Changed the notice Claude gets when the WebSearch budget is used up to also tell it not to query search engines in a browser or through computer use
  • Changed the axScreenReader setting and CLAUDE_AX_SCREEN_READER in a settings env block to apply only from user, managed or --settings settings (since 2.1.305)
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed checkout hooks to be stopped after 30 minutes by default, failing the session's setup; if yours needs longer, raise --checkout-hook-timeout-min or set it to 0
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the certificate file built for Anthropic-managed git to filter its trusted certificates as the CLI does; a [runner:warn] line gives the number left out
  • [VSCode] Added a notice on the microphone button when voice dictation stops by itself (15 seconds without recognized speech, or the 2-minute limit), saying why and that the text so far is kept
  • [VSCode] Fixed a long prompt expanded with Show more covering the whole chat panel: a pinned prompt is now capped at 40% of the panel and scrolls
  • [VSCode] Fixed part of a list item or table cell with LaTeX math pasting as a new list or table in rich text editors
  • [VSCode] Fixed dictation failing behind a TLS-inspecting proxy when NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS is set only in ~/.claude/settings.json; it now also follows CLAUDE_CODE_CERT_STORE
  • [VSCode] Changed the "still open somewhere else" notice to also cover a Claude process left over from an extension restart, which usually ends on its own within about 10 minutes
  • [VSCode] Changed voice dictation to filter its trusted certificates as the CLI does
  • [VSCode] Changed the extension's own requests to filter their trusted certificates as the CLI does, and to trust the NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS file named in the environment or in user settings
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the repository picker saying "No repositories match" while a search was still running; it now shows "Searching…" until the results arrive
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the "Waiting for a runner" status on self-hosted environments being cut off; with on-demand runners it now counts up from your last message and shows failed attempts
  • [Code Review] Added @claude review stop (also off and pause) to Code Review, ending an @claude review always subscription on a pull request without starting a new review

items.title: DIAL: Steerable Language Models with Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels
items.summary: When a user says "Keep it short", how short should the LLM's response be? More generally, users and applications require different levels of instruction adherence, but prompting does not reliably provide fine-grained control over them. We therefore study "steerable language models" that provide fine-grained numerical control over the degree to which models follow general instructions specified in text. However, existing approaches do not jointly offer fine-grained control, efficiency, and scalability across diverse instructions. To address this gap, we introduce DIAL (Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels) to achieve all three properties. For fine-grained control, we perform classifier-free guidance (CFG) with a frozen LLM to provide training signals for on-policy distillation of instruction adherence at different levels. For efficiency, we design a lightweight steering adapter that uses a classifier over the LLM's hidden states to compute a closed-form steering edit. The classifier adaptively sets the steering magnitude at each token based on the target adherence level, while accounting for the geometry of the LLM's hidden states to preserve response coherence. For scalability, the classifier is text-conditioned, allowing a shared adapter to support new instructions without per-instruction fitting, and training requires only instruction and request text. Evaluation across multiple LLM families shows that DIAL achieves a competitive balance between concept expression and response fluency, with concept scores increasing monotonically across adherence levels. We introduce SteerIF, an instruction-only dataset of 98, 625 concept, persona, verifiable, and descriptive instructions. When trained on SteerIF, DIAL provides fine-grained control over personas and, when combined with prompting, improves verifiable instruction following.

items.title: Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration
items.summary: Research on sycophancy asks whether large language models (LLMs) bend towards what their users want to hear. We ask the reverse question: when an LLM is confident, consistent, and wrong, do users bend towards it? In a within-subjects experiment, 32 participants learned up to five science topics by chatting with five assistants built on the same model (GPT-5-mini). Unknown to participants, each assistant's briefing had 0, 25, 50, 75, or 100% of its facts replaced by plausible falsehoods, and every assistant spoke with full confidence. A surprise quiz after each topic offered the correct fact, the planted falsehood, and two distractors, with a confidence rating for every answer. Across 104 quizzes and 1,040 answers, scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10, and the planted option was chosen on 60% of falsified items against 11% of correctly taught ones (odds ratio 12.5). Transcript coding showed that whenever the assistant stated a falsehood, it was adopted about 65% of the time at every falsification level. Absorbed falsehoods were held with high confidence (8.4/10), the modeled confidence advantage of right over wrong answers vanished, and the discrimination of confidence for correctness fell from an AUROC of 0.70 to chance, while post-task trust ratings barely moved. Participants tended to return to the chat more when the assistant was worse, but returning went with more absorption, not less, and 30% of all turns pasted quiz questions back to the source being checked. The assistant itself was almost never sycophantic and never conceded under pushback. We introduce a baseline-corrected Human Deference Index to quantify this human-side sycophancy and argue that trustworthiness is a property of the human-AI pair, that sycophancy evaluations should measure both directions, and that learning interfaces must make reliability legible claim by claim.

items.title: Expanding Claude availability and deployment choice on Google Cloud
items.summary:
Every organization has unique requirements for building and scaling generative AI. At Google Cloud, we are committed to giving developers model choice and architectural flexibility to run workloads however they need.

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of an Anthropic-managed deployment option for Claude Models on Google Cloud. This gives teams more choice in how they run their models, helping them consolidate AI workloads on Google Cloud alongside our existingGoogle-managed deployment option. 

Both options deliver the same frontier models on day zero, the same pricing, and the same Google Cloud billing. The difference comes down to who acts as your data processor and whether you need access to the new Claude platform features when they launch:

[NEW] Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed)

Delivers day-zero access to Claude models and Claude Platform features such as Claude Managed Agents (beta), skills, and code execution. Anthropic operates the stack as the data processor on Google Cloud infrastructure under Anthropic’s terms of service, while organizations authenticate with Google Cloud IAM, maintain Cloud Audit Logging, and consolidate spend under their existing Google Cloud billing and eligible commitments.

Learn more: Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic-managed).

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed)

Continues to deliver day-zero access to the latest Claude models with strict governance, compliance, and sovereignty requirements. Google Cloud operates as the data processor under existing customer agreements, providing VPC Service Controls, Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK), and data residency in the U.S., EU, and APAC. New Claude Platform features roll out over time as they are integrated into the Google-managed infrastructure. Teams also benefit from native integrations with Google Cloud services like BigQuery and Model Armor, along with standard billing and eligible commitment drawdown. 

Learn more: Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed)

Comparing deployment options

 

Feature

Anthropic-managed

Google-managed

Model availability

Available on Day 0

Available on Day 0

First-party tools and betas 

Available on Day 0

Google Cloud (under existing Google Cloud customer agreements)

Pricing & commitments

Standard pricing (draws down eligible Google Cloud commitments)

No matter how you choose to deploy, you can access Anthropic's latest frontier models on Google Cloud, including Claude Fable 5.1, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and Opus 5.5, with new platform features available immediately on the Anthropic-managed option and rolling out on the Google-managed option once integrated. This gives developers the full spectrum of reasoning, coding, and multi-modal capabilities with Google Cloud IAM and Marketplace billing. Get started.
